ARTICLE XI — THE HERITAGE GRANTS DIVISION

11.1 The Heritage Grants Division shall be responsible for the administration of grants made by the Bureau for the purpose of supporting genealogical research, the preservation of family records, and the publication of works advancing the knowledge of Singapore’s family heritage.

Public enquiries reached a new high of 8,214, an increase of 11% over the previous year. The demand for family history services continues to grow as Singaporeans become more interested in their roots. The Bureau is grateful for the patience of the public as the indexing project proceeds; the backlog of written enquiries, however, remains a concern.

2. GENEALOGICAL RECORDS AND ACCESS SERVICES

The Bureau holds the largest collection of genealogical materials in Singapore, comprising:

- Registry of Births and Deaths transcripts (selected years, 1889–1960)
- Church baptism and marriage registers (microfilm)
- Temple and clan association records
- Cemetery inscriptions and burial records
- Oral history interview transcripts
- Family histories and genealogical charts donated by the public
- Colonial-era census returns (selected districts)

2.1 The Digital Indexing Project

The most important development of the year was the commencement of digital indexing of genealogical records. The project began on 1 July 1985, following approval of the necessary funding in the 1985/86 budget. The goal is to create a searchable computer index of all major record series held by the Bureau, to be made available to the public in the reading room and, eventually, through remote access.

The project will proceed in phases. Phase One, which began in July, covers the Registry of Births and Deaths transcripts for the years 1889–1920. This is the most heavily used series in the collection. The work is being carried out by a team of four indexers under the supervision of the Senior Archivist (Records). The indexers use a data-entry system developed in-house, which includes fields for name, date of birth or death, place, and source reference.

The project is expected to take approximately three years to complete for all major series. The Bureau is mindful of the need to balance the demands of indexing with the continued provision of reference services. No reduction in public service hours is planned.

Progress to date (as at 31 December 1985):

- Records indexed: 48,320
- Records awaiting verification: 6,150
- Records rejected as illegible: 1,020

The Bureau acknowledges the cooperation of the National Archives in lending additional microfilm readers for the duration of the project.

2.2 Reading Room Services

The reading room at the Bureau’s premises at 12 Stamford Road continues to be the primary point of access to the collection. Opening hours remain unchanged: Monday to Friday, 9.00 am to 5.00 pm, and Saturday, 9.00 am to 1.00 pm.

The reading room is equipped with six microfilm readers, two microfiche readers, and, since October, one computer terminal for the digital index. The terminal is available on a first-come, first-served basis. Members of the public may also request a printout of index entries at a cost of $0.50 per page.

2.3 Written Enquiries

The Bureau received 2,847 written enquiries in 1985, of which 2,103 were answered within six weeks. The remainder were delayed owing to the need to consult records held off-site. The Bureau apologises for these delays and is working to reduce them.

Enquiry topics in 1985, by percentage:

- Birth and baptism records: 38%
- Marriage records: 22%
- Death and burial records: 19%
- Immigration and naturalisation: 12%
- Other: 9%

2.4 Records Conservation

A programme of conservation treatment for fragile volumes continued throughout the year. A total of 214 volumes were treated, including 86 volumes of Chinese clan association records and 54 volumes of Malay marriage registers. The Bureau is grateful to the National Library for the use of its conservation workshop.
4. THE FAMILY HISTORY DIGITIZATION INITIATIVE

4.1 Establishment and Purpose

The Family History Digitization Initiative (the Initiative) was established on 1 July 1985. The Initiative is a cooperative programme under which the Bureau, together with the National Archives and the National Library, will convert the Bureau's principal finding aids and indexes to machine-readable form, and subsequently capture digital images of the most heavily used record series. The objective is to reduce wear on original volumes, to permit searching of the index by computer, and to prepare the Bureau's holdings for the eventual transfer of reference services to a new facility.

The Initiative was formally announced in the Minister's speech at the Bureau's twentieth anniversary dinner on 28 June 1985. The Minister noted that the Bureau's records were "a national asset of the first importance" and that the digitization programme would "secure these records for the use of future generations." A small steering committee, chaired by the Deputy Director, was constituted in July. The committee met monthly.

4.2 Scope of Work

The first phase of the Initiative covers the following series:

- The civil registration index, 1872–1940 (approximately 1.2 million entries)
- The baptism and marriage registers of the principal Christian churches, 1826–1900
- The Chinese clan association records, as listed in the Bureau's published guide
- The Malay marriage registers, 1900–1940

Photographic reproduction of the registers will be undertaken only after the index entries for the relevant series have been verified. The Bureau has procured two digital cameras and a dedicated workstation for this purpose. The cameras were delivered in September and have been tested on a sample of the church registers. Image quality has been judged acceptable for the majority of volumes, although a small number of very dark or tightly bound volumes will require additional lighting and will be treated as a separate work package.

The annual report for 1985 states that the Family History Digitization Initiative had launch_date 1985-07-01. Record status: historical.

4.3 Progress in the Second Half of 1985

The Initiative's first working day was 1 July 1985. In the six months to 31 December, the following milestones were reached:

- Steering committee constituted: 18 July
- Digitization procedures manual issued: 30 August
- First camera delivered: 12 September
- Indexing of the civil registration index, 1872–1900, completed: 15 November
- Digital images captured of the baptism registers of the three oldest congregations: 20 December

The indexing of the civil registration index for 1901–1940 is expected to be completed by June 1986. The church registers for the remaining congregations will be photographed in the course of 1986.

4.4 Staffing

The Initiative is staffed by two full-time indexers, seconded from the National Archives, and one full-time photographer, recruited in August. The photographer was trained on the Bureau's premises for one week. In addition, one member of the Bureau's own staff has been assigned half-time to the Initiative to handle correspondence and to maintain the log of work completed.

The Bureau wishes to record its appreciation for the cooperation of the National Archives, which has also provided the loan of two extra microfilm readers for the duration of the project. These readers have been in continuous use since October.

The closure was implemented in two phases. The eastern and western offices closed on 30 September 2002, while the northern office, which had the largest outreach programme, closed on 31 December 2002. All staff were offered redeployment to headquarters or to other government agencies. Of the 24 staff affected, 18 accepted redeployment to the Bureau, 4 transferred to other agencies, and 2 retired.

### 3.3 The Centralisation of Grant Review

The centralisation of grant review was completed on 31 December 2002. From that date, all grant applications were processed by a single unit at headquarters. This unit, the Grants and Community Programmes Section, was established under the Deputy Director (Public Services) and comprised five officers: a Senior Archivist (Grants), two Archivists, one Executive Officer, and one clerical officer.

The centralised process introduced a standardised application form, a fixed review cycle, and a single point of contact for applicants. Previously, each regional office had its own application form and review schedule, which had caused confusion among applicants and delays in processing.

The new process was as follows:

1. Applications were received by the Grants and Community Programmes Section, either by post or by email.
2. Each application was logged and acknowledged within 5 working days.
3. Applications were assessed against published eligibility criteria by an Archivist, with the Senior Archivist (Grants) providing a second review.
4. Recommendations were submitted to a monthly Grants Review Panel, chaired by the Deputy Director (Public Services).
5. Applicants were notified of the outcome within 10 working days of the Panel's decision.

The first meeting of the Grants Review Panel was held on 28 January 2003. In the first quarter of 2003, the Section received 42 applications, of which 31 were approved.

### 3.4 Impact on Services

The closure of the regional offices had a noticeable impact on the Bureau's operations. Public enquiries handled at the regional offices were redirected to the headquarters reference room, which saw a 15% increase in visitor numbers in the first quarter of 2003. To manage the increased demand, the reference room extended its opening hours on Wednesday evenings and Saturday afternoons.

The outreach programmes formerly run by the regional offices were not discontinued entirely. Instead, they were reorganised as a travelling programme, with Bureau staff visiting community centres and schools on a scheduled basis. The travelling programme was initially less extensive than the regional outreach had been, but it was expanded from April 2003 following positive feedback from participating communities.

The microfilm reading room at headquarters was expanded to accommodate the additional readers previously available at the regional offices. Six additional microfilm readers were installed in November 2002, and a second digital imaging workstation was added in January 2003.

### 3.5 Financial Implications

The closure of the regional offices resulted in significant savings. The Bureau's premises and utilities expenditure for 2003 was 22% lower than in 2001, despite the expansion of the headquarters reference room. The savings were partly offset by the costs of the travelling programme and the additional equipment, but the net effect was a reduction in operating expenditure.

During 2018, the Office completed a systematic review of the master name index entries for the birth registers, 1872–1923. The review was initiated following the identification of a systematic error in the transcription of Chinese dialect names in the 1900–1915 period. In the original registers, names were recorded in a variety of romanisation systems, and the indexers had, in some cases, standardised the spelling to the Mandarin pinyin form. This was incorrect, as the registers themselves use the romanisation given by the informant at the time of registration.

The review covered 18,340 entries. Of these, 1,276 entries were corrected. The corrections were made to the index only; the scanned images of the original registers were not altered. The corrected entries have been flagged in the index with a “Q” marker, which indicates that the entry has been reviewed and verified against the original register image.

ARTICLE XI — THE HERITAGE GRANTS DIVISION

11.1 The Heritage Grants Division shall be responsible for the administration of grants made by the Bureau for the purpose of supporting genealogical research, the preservation of family records, and the publication of works advancing the knowledge of Singapore’s family heritage.

11.2 The functions of the Heritage Grants Division shall include:

(a) receiving and processing applications for grants;

(b) assessing applications with the advice of the Grants Advisory Panel constituted under Article XII;

(c) disbursing grants in accordance with the terms and conditions approved by the Commissioner;

(d) monitoring the progress of grant-funded projects and requiring the submission of reports and accounts;

(e) recovering grants, or any part thereof, where the conditions of the grant have not been fulfilled.

11.3 The Heritage Grants Division shall be headed by the Registrar of Grants, who shall be appointed by the Commissioner and who shall hold office for a term of three years, renewable.

11.4 The Heritage Grants Division shall maintain a public register of all grants awarded, including the name of the grantee, the purpose of the grant, the amount awarded, and the date of award.

ARTICLE XII — THE GRANTS ADVISORY PANEL

12.1 There shall be a Grants Advisory Panel consisting of not less than five and not more than nine members, appointed by the Commissioner for a term of two years.

12.2 The members of the Panel shall be persons with knowledge and experience in genealogy, history, archival science, or community affairs.

12.3 The Panel shall elect its own Chairman from among its members.

12.4 The Panel shall meet at least once in every quarter and may invite the Registrar of Grants or other officers of the Bureau to attend its meetings for the purpose of providing information.

12.5 The Panel shall advise the Commissioner on the merits of applications for grants and may recommend conditions to be attached to any grant.

ARTICLE XIII — THE BUREAU’S LIAISON OFFICERS

13.1 The Commissioner may appoint officers of the Bureau to serve as liaison officers for the purpose of maintaining contact with family associations, clan societies, religious organisations, and other bodies concerned with family heritage.

13.2 Liaison officers shall, in the discharge of their duties:

(a) assist such bodies in the identification and preservation of records of genealogical value;

(b) encourage the deposit of such records with the Bureau;

(c) report to the Records and Access Division on the existence and location of records that may be of interest to the Bureau.

13.3 Liaison officers shall not have authority to bind the Bureau to any expenditure or commitment without the prior approval of the Commissioner.

ARTICLE XIV — FINANCE

14.1 The funds of the Bureau shall consist of:

(a) moneys appropriated by Parliament for the purposes of the Bureau;

(b) moneys received by way of grants, gifts, or bequests;

(c) fees and charges levied for services rendered by the Bureau;

(d) all other moneys lawfully received by the Bureau.

14.2 The accounts of the Bureau shall be kept in such form as the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry may direct, and shall be audited annually by the Auditor-General.

14.3 The Commissioner shall, not later than 31 July in each year, submit to the Minister a report on the activities of the Bureau during the preceding financial year, together with the audited accounts.

Public enquiries reached a new high of 8,214, an increase of 11% over the previous year. The demand for family history services continues to grow as Singaporeans become more interested in their roots. The Bureau is grateful for the patience of the public as the indexing project proceeds; the backlog of written enquiries, however, remains a concern.

2. GENEALOGICAL RECORDS AND ACCESS SERVICES

The Bureau holds the largest collection of genealogical materials in Singapore, comprising:

- Registry of Births and Deaths transcripts (selected years, 1889–1960)
- Church baptism and marriage registers (microfilm)
- Temple and clan association records
- Cemetery inscriptions and burial records
- Oral history interview transcripts
- Family histories and genealogical charts donated by the public
- Colonial-era census returns (selected districts)

2.1 The Digital Indexing Project

The most important development of the year was the commencement of digital indexing of genealogical records. The project began on 1 July 1985, following approval of the necessary funding in the 1985/86 budget. The goal is to create a searchable computer index of all major record series held by the Bureau, to be made available to the public in the reading room and, eventually, through remote access.

The project will proceed in phases. Phase One, which began in July, covers the Registry of Births and Deaths transcripts for the years 1889–1920. This is the most heavily used series in the collection. The work is being carried out by a team of four indexers under the supervision of the Senior Archivist (Records). The indexers use a data-entry system developed in-house, which includes fields for name, date of birth or death, place, and source reference.

The project is expected to take approximately three years to complete for all major series. The Bureau is mindful of the need to balance the demands of indexing with the continued provision of reference services. No reduction in public service hours is planned.

Progress to date (as at 31 December 1985):

- Records indexed: 48,320
- Records awaiting verification: 6,150
- Records rejected as illegible: 1,020

Annual Report 1985 reports_digital_indexing_start 1985-07-01. Record status: historical.

The Bureau acknowledges the cooperation of the National Archives in lending additional microfilm readers for the duration of the project.

2.2 Reading Room Services

The reading room at the Bureau’s premises at 12 Stamford Road continues to be the primary point of access to the collection. Opening hours remain unchanged: Monday to Friday, 9.00 am to 5.00 pm, and Saturday, 9.00 am to 1.00 pm.

The reading room is equipped with six microfilm readers, two microfiche readers, and, since October, one computer terminal for the digital index. The terminal is available on a first-come, first-served basis. Members of the public may also request a printout of index entries at a cost of $0.50 per page.

2.3 Written Enquiries

The Bureau received 2,847 written enquiries in 1985, of which 2,103 were answered within six weeks. The remainder were delayed owing to the need to consult records held off-site. The Bureau apologises for these delays and is working to reduce them.

Enquiry topics in 1985, by percentage:

- Birth and baptism records: 38%
- Marriage records: 22%
- Death and burial records: 19%
- Immigration and naturalisation: 12%
- Other: 9%

2.4 Records Conservation

A programme of conservation treatment for fragile volumes continued throughout the year. A total of 214 volumes were treated, including 86 volumes of Chinese clan association records and 54 volumes of Malay marriage registers. The Bureau is grateful to the National Library for the use of its conservation workshop.

4. THE FAMILY HISTORY DIGITIZATION INITIATIVE

4.1 Establishment and Purpose

The Family History Digitization Initiative (the Initiative) was established on 1 July 1985. The Initiative is a cooperative programme under which the Bureau, together with the National Archives and the National Library, will convert the Bureau's principal finding aids and indexes to machine-readable form, and subsequently capture digital images of the most heavily used record series. The objective is to reduce wear on original volumes, to permit searching of the index by computer, and to prepare the Bureau's holdings for the eventual transfer of reference services to a new facility.

The Initiative was formally announced in the Minister's speech at the Bureau's twentieth anniversary dinner on 28 June 1985. The Minister noted that the Bureau's records were "a national asset of the first importance" and that the digitization programme would "secure these records for the use of future generations." A small steering committee, chaired by the Deputy Director, was constituted in July. The committee met monthly.

4.2 Scope of Work

The first phase of the Initiative covers the following series:

- The civil registration index, 1872–1940 (approximately 1.2 million entries)
- The baptism and marriage registers of the principal Christian churches, 1826–1900
- The Chinese clan association records, as listed in the Bureau's published guide
- The Malay marriage registers, 1900–1940

Photographic reproduction of the registers will be undertaken only after the index entries for the relevant series have been verified. The Bureau has procured two digital cameras and a dedicated workstation for this purpose. The cameras were delivered in September and have been tested on a sample of the church registers. Image quality has been judged acceptable for the majority of volumes, although a small number of very dark or tightly bound volumes will require additional lighting and will be treated as a separate work package.

The annual report for 1985 states that the Family History Digitization Initiative had launch_date 1985-07-01. Record status: historical.

4.3 Progress in the Second Half of 1985

The Initiative's first working day was 1 July 1985. In the six months to 31 December, the following milestones were reached:

- Steering committee constituted: 18 July
- Digitization procedures manual issued: 30 August
- First camera delivered: 12 September
- Indexing of the civil registration index, 1872–1900, completed: 15 November
- Digital images captured of the baptism registers of the three oldest congregations: 20 December

The indexing of the civil registration index for 1901–1940 is expected to be completed by June 1986. The church registers for the remaining congregations will be photographed in the course of 1986.

4.4 Staffing

The Initiative is staffed by two full-time indexers, seconded from the National Archives, and one full-time photographer, recruited in August. The photographer was trained on the Bureau's premises for one week. In addition, one member of the Bureau's own staff has been assigned half-time to the Initiative to handle correspondence and to maintain the log of work completed.

The Bureau wishes to record its appreciation for the cooperation of the National Archives, which has also provided the loan of two extra microfilm readers for the duration of the project. These readers have been in continuous use since October.

The closure was implemented in two phases. The eastern and western offices closed on 30 September 2002, while the northern office, which had the largest outreach programme, closed on 31 December 2002. All staff were offered redeployment to headquarters or to other government agencies. Of the 24 staff affected, 18 accepted redeployment to the Bureau, 4 transferred to other agencies, and 2 retired.

### 3.3 The Centralisation of Grant Review

The centralisation of grant review was completed on 31 December 2002. From that date, all grant applications were processed by a single unit at headquarters. This unit, the Grants and Community Programmes Section, was established under the Deputy Director (Public Services) and comprised five officers: a Senior Archivist (Grants), two Archivists, one Executive Officer, and one clerical officer.

The centralised process introduced a standardised application form, a fixed review cycle, and a single point of contact for applicants. Previously, each regional office had its own application form and review schedule, which had caused confusion among applicants and delays in processing.

The new process was as follows:

1. Applications were received by the Grants and Community Programmes Section, either by post or by email.
2. Each application was logged and acknowledged within 5 working days.
3. Applications were assessed against published eligibility criteria by an Archivist, with the Senior Archivist (Grants) providing a second review.
4. Recommendations were submitted to a monthly Grants Review Panel, chaired by the Deputy Director (Public Services).
5. Applicants were notified of the outcome within 10 working days of the Panel's decision.

The first meeting of the Grants Review Panel was held on 28 January 2003. In the first quarter of 2003, the Section received 42 applications, of which 31 were approved.

Annual Report 2002 reports_centralization_completion 2002-12-31. Record status: historical.

### 3.4 Impact on Services

The closure of the regional offices had a noticeable impact on the Bureau's operations. Public enquiries handled at the regional offices were redirected to the headquarters reference room, which saw a 15% increase in visitor numbers in the first quarter of 2003. To manage the increased demand, the reference room extended its opening hours on Wednesday evenings and Saturday afternoons.

The outreach programmes formerly run by the regional offices were not discontinued entirely. Instead, they were reorganised as a travelling programme, with Bureau staff visiting community centres and schools on a scheduled basis. The travelling programme was initially less extensive than the regional outreach had been, but it was expanded from April 2003 following positive feedback from participating communities.

The microfilm reading room at headquarters was expanded to accommodate the additional readers previously available at the regional offices. Six additional microfilm readers were installed in November 2002, and a second digital imaging workstation was added in January 2003.

### 3.5 Financial Implications

The closure of the regional offices resulted in significant savings. The Bureau's premises and utilities expenditure for 2003 was 22% lower than in 2001, despite the expansion of the headquarters reference room. The savings were partly offset by the costs of the travelling programme and the additional equipment, but the net effect was a reduction in operating expenditure.

1. CHAIRMAN'S MESSAGE

The past year has been one of consolidation and quiet renewal. With the closure of the regional offices completed in late 2002, the Bureau has now settled into a single-site operation at our headquarters on Stamford Road. I am pleased to report that the transition, though demanding, has been handled with professionalism by all concerned. Public services have not only been maintained but in several areas strengthened, and the travelling programme has exceeded our initial expectations in both reach and reception.

The Grants Review Panel, established in January 2003, has brought a new discipline to the distribution of project funds. The Panel's careful scrutiny ensures that every dollar is directed toward work that genuinely advances the preservation and understanding of family heritage in Singapore. In the first year of its operation, the Panel approved 31 of 42 applications received in the first quarter alone, a rate that speaks to the quality of proposals being submitted by the community.

We enter 2004 with a clear sense of purpose. The Bureau's role is not merely to store records but to connect people with their past. The projects described in this report, from the digitisation of pre-war photographs to the oral history workshops in HDB heartlands, all serve that central mission.

Tan Cheng Huat
Chairman
Singapore Family Heritage Bureau

- Completion of the regional office closure programme, with all records and services consolidated at headquarters by December 2002.
- Establishment of the Grants Review Panel in January 2003; 31 of 42 first-quarter applications approved.
- Launch of the travelling outreach programme in January 2003, expanded from April 2003 following positive community feedback.

# ANNUAL REPORT OF THE SINGAPORE FAMILY HERITAGE BUREAU

## FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2003/2004

---

### 1. CHAIRMAN'S STATEMENT

The past year has been one of consolidation and quiet transformation. As the Bureau settled into its fully consolidated headquarters operation, we have been able to turn our attention outward—toward the communities we serve and the collections we hold in trust.

Three developments give me particular confidence as we look ahead. First, the Grants Review Panel has brought a new discipline and transparency to our funding decisions. Second, the travelling outreach programme has carried our services beyond the reading rooms and into the heartlands, where family history is lived rather than merely researched. Third, our digitisation efforts have begun to unlock collections that were previously accessible only to the most determined researcher.

None of this would have been possible without the dedication of our staff, whose professionalism during the office closure programme was exemplary. I thank them, and I thank the many volunteers who continue to assist with our oral history projects and community exhibitions.

The year ahead will see the Bureau deepen its engagement with schools and with the Malay and Indian communities, whose archival traditions deserve greater representation in our collections. We will also complete the migration of our catalogue to the new integrated library system, which will for the first time allow users to search across our holdings and those of the National Library Board from a single interface.

The Bureau's mission remains what it has always been: to help every Singaporean family find its story, and to preserve those stories for the generations that will follow.

Tan Cheng Huat
Chairman
Singapore Family Heritage Bureau

- Full consolidation of operations at headquarters completed; regional office closure programme closed out with no loss of records.

- Travelling outreach programme visited 23 community clubs, schools, and libraries across the island; 1,400+ members of the public attended introductory workshops.

5A. REVISED DIGITISATION TARGET

In the 2017 annual report, the Office stated that the overall digitisation programme would be completed by December 2019. That target is revised. The current estimate, based on the indexing rates achieved in the fourth quarter of 2018, is that the programme will be substantially complete by June 2020. The delay is attributable to two factors: (a) the decision to include the estate duty files in the programme, which added approximately 3,200 records; and (b) the higher-than-expected volume of corrections to the master name index arising from the quality-control review of the birth registers (see Section 6 below).

The revised target has been discussed with the Ministry and the Office’s Board of Management. No change to the approved budget is required, as the additional work is being absorbed by the existing processing teams.

6. QUALITY CONTROL AND INDEX CORRECTIONS

During 2018, the Office completed a systematic review of the master name index entries for the birth registers, 1872–1923. The review was initiated following the identification of a systematic error in the transcription of Chinese dialect names in the 1900–1915 period. In the original registers, names were recorded in a variety of romanisation systems, and the indexers had, in some cases, standardised the spelling to the Mandarin pinyin form. This was incorrect, as the registers themselves use the romanisation given by the informant at the time of registration.

The review covered 18,340 entries. Of these, 1,276 entries were corrected. The corrections were made to the index only; the scanned images of the original registers were not altered. The corrected entries have been flagged in the index with a “Q” marker, which indicates that the entry has been reviewed and verified against the original register image.
